name: Chrysler / Valiant Australia
overview: Chrysler Australia Ltd was established in June 1951 following Chrysler Corporation's acquisition of Adelaide coachbuilder Richards Industries. Operating from its monumental manufacturing complex at Tonsley Park and engine foundry at Lonsdale in South Australia, Chrysler was the third of the 'Big Three' Australian domestic automakers alongside Holden and Ford. In January 1962, Chrysler launched the revolutionary Valiant (R-Series), whose 145 hp Slant-6 engine instantly out-accelerated and outperformed every rival on Australian roads. In 1970, Chrysler Australia's local engineering team created the iconic HEMI-6 engine, featuring hemispherical combustion chambers and producing massive torque. The following year, Chrysler introduced the VH Valiant Charger—backed by the unforgettable 'Hey Charger!' advertising campaign—whose triple-Weber E49 'Six Pack' became the fastest-accelerating Australian production car for over a decade. Facing financial distress in the late 1970s, Chrysler Australia sold its operations to Mitsubishi Motors Corporation in 1980, creating Mitsubishi Motors Australia Limited (MMAL). The Chrysler brand was later re-introduced as an American import arm (300C, PT Cruiser, Voyager) before departing Australia in 2021.
australian_history:
Chrysler's Australian heritage began in the 1920s through T.J. Richards & Sons, an Adelaide coachbuilder constructing bodies for Dodge, DeSoto, and Plymouth chassis. In June 1951, Chrysler Corporation acquired Richards Industries to establish Chrysler Australia Ltd, based initially at Mile End and Keswick. In 1957, Chrysler introduced the Chrysler Royal (AP1, AP2, AP3), an Australian-unique evolution of 1953-54 Plymouth architecture featuring flamboyant tail fins and push-button automatic transmissions.

In January 1962, Chrysler dramatically altered the Australian automotive landscape by assembling 1,008 units of the American compact Plymouth Valiant as the 'R-Series'. Powered by a 225 cubic-inch (3.7-litre) 'Slant-6' engine producing 145 bhp, it completely outclassed the 75 bhp Holden EK and 85 bhp Ford Falcon, selling out within days. In 1963, Chrysler opened its sprawling, billion-dollar Tonsley Park plant in suburban Adelaide and introduced the first fully manufactured Australian Valiant, the AP5 (Australian Production 5), followed by the AP6 which introduced the 273ci V8—the first V8 offered in an Australian family car.

Under chief engineer David Giles, Chrysler Australia invested $22 million developing an all-new six-cylinder engine tailored for Australian conditions. Debuting in the 1970 VG series, the HEMI-6 (available in 215ci, 245ci, and 265ci displacements) eliminated the pushrod angles of conventional OHV engines and incorporated hemispherical combustion chambers, yielding immense volumetric efficiency. In August 1971, Chrysler launched the VH series—the first Valiant designed and styled completely in Australia—headlined by the short-wheelbase Valiant Charger coupe. Engineered by John Ellis, the Charger won the 1971 Wheels Car of the Year and spawned the homologation specials E38 (280 bhp) and the legendary E49 (302 bhp, triple twin-choke Weber 45 DCOE carburettors, 4-speed Borg-Warner manual). The E49 Charger held the Australian production car quarter-mile record (14.4 seconds) for over a decade.

In the mid-1970s, Chrysler introduced the Centura (KB/KC), grafting the Australian Hemi-6 into the French Simca 180 bodyshell. However, high development costs, the 1973 oil crisis, and parent Chrysler Corporation's financial crisis forced restructuring. In 1979-1980, Mitsubishi Corporation acquired Chrysler Australia's Tonsley Park and Lonsdale facilities, transitioning production to the Chrysler Sigma and Colt before renaming the company Mitsubishi Motors Australia Limited (MMAL) in October 1980. The last Australian Valiant—a silver CM Regal sedan—rolled off the Tonsley Park line on 28 August 1981. In 1994, Chrysler returned to Australia as an importer under Chrysler/DaimlerChrysler/FCA, enjoying major success with the Chrysler 300C large sedan, PT Cruiser, Crossfire, and Grand Voyager before retiring the brand in Australia in November 2021.

models.name: Chrysler Valiant
models.overview: The Chrysler Valiant was the spirited contender of the Australian family car triumvirate alongside the Holden Kingswood and Ford Falcon. Manufactured at Chrysler Australia's sprawling Tonsley Park complex in Adelaide from 1962 to 1981 across 13 series (R, S, AP5, AP6, VC, VE, VF, VG, VH, VJ, VK, CL, CM), the Valiant established an enduring reputation for unmatched horsepower, introducing the 145 hp Slant-6 in 1962, Australia's first family car V8 in 1965, the world-renowned Australian-engineered HEMI-6 in 1970, and pioneering Electronic Lean Burn (ELB) computer management.

models.name: Chrysler Centura
models.overview: The Chrysler Centura (KB and KC series) was Chrysler Australia's audacious weapon to conquer the mid-size family car market dominated by the Holden Torana and Ford Cortina. Assembled at Tonsley Park in Adelaide, Chrysler imported European Simca 180 bodyshells from France and undertook radical local re-engineering to shoehorn Chrysler Australia's mighty Australian-cast 3.5L (Hemi 215) and 4.0L (Hemi 245) pushrod straight-six engines, alongside a French 2.0L Simca 4-cylinder. With 123 kW (165 hp) and 319 Nm of torque propelling a compact 1,200 kg body, the Hemi 245 Centura was an astonishing sleeper muscle sedan, sprinting from 0-100 km/h in under 9 seconds and completing the standing quarter-mile in 16.5 seconds. 19,770 units were produced across the KB (1975-1977) and updated KC (1977-1978).

models.name: Chrysler / Mitsubishi Sigma
models.overview: The Chrysler Sigma—later renamed Mitsubishi Sigma after Mitsubishi acquired Chrysler Australia in 1980—was the undisputed king of Australia's four-cylinder family car market across the late 1970s and 1980s. Manufactured at Tonsley Park in Adelaide, the Sigma (GE, GH, GJ, GK, GN) dethroned traditional six-cylinder cars by offering expansive interior space, European-influenced styling, four-wheel coil spring suspension, and revolutionary 'Silent Shaft' counter-rotating balance shafts in its Australian-cast Astron 1.85L, 2.0L, and 2.6L engines. The GH series introduced the legendary limited-edition Sigma Turbo in 1981 (Australia's first locally built turbocharged production car), while the 1982 GJ series spawned the celebrated Peter Wherrett Special. Over 300,000 Sigmas were built in Adelaide before making way for the Magna.

models.name: Chrysler Valiant Charger
models.overview: The Chrysler Valiant Charger is one of the most charismatic muscle cars in Australian history. Launched in August 1971 with the memorable 'Hey Charger!' television advertising campaign, the Charger was built on a shortened 105-inch wheelbase with stunning fastback proportions, winning the 1971 Wheels Car of the Year award. Immortalized by the legendary Bathurst homologation specials—the E38 (280 bhp) and the triple-Weber E49 'Six Pack' (302 bhp)—the Charger was the fastest-accelerating Australian production car for over a decade, holding the standing quarter-mile record at 14.4 seconds.

models.name: Dodge Phoenix
models.overview: The Dodge Phoenix was Chrysler Australia's grand American luxury flagship from 1960 to 1973. Conceived to compete head-on with the Ford Galaxie and Chevrolet Impala/Bel Air in the prestige government, executive, and pastoralist market, the Phoenix was assembled in Adelaide from North American CKD packs, using Dodge Dart/Polara, Plymouth Fury, and Chrysler bodies married to bespoke factory right-hand drive Plymouth dashboards. Spanning the early finned PD/RD series through to the majestic 'fuselage'-bodied models of 1969-1973, every Phoenix was powered by burly American Chrysler V8 engines—predominantly the 318ci (5.2L) 'Poly' and 'LA' small-block V8s, and the optional 383ci (6.3L) 'B-block' Big Block V8 in the opulent Phoenix 400 Hardtop. Sumptuously appointed with Torqueflite 3-speed automatic transmissions, power steering, push-button radios, and deep plush interiors, the Phoenix was the undisputed car of choice for Australian politicians, judges, and graziers.

centura.name: Chrysler Centura
centura.overview: The Chrysler Centura (KB and KC series) was Chrysler Australia's audacious weapon to conquer the mid-size family car market dominated by the Holden Torana and Ford Cortina. Assembled at Tonsley Park in Adelaide, Chrysler imported European Simca 180 bodyshells from France and undertook radical local re-engineering to shoehorn Chrysler Australia's mighty Australian-cast 3.5L (Hemi 215) and 4.0L (Hemi 245) pushrod straight-six engines, alongside a French 2.0L Simca 4-cylinder. With 123 kW (165 hp) and 319 Nm of torque propelling a compact 1,200 kg body, the Hemi 245 Centura was an astonishing sleeper muscle sedan, sprinting from 0-100 km/h in under 9 seconds and completing the standing quarter-mile in 16.5 seconds. 19,770 units were produced across the KB (1975-1977) and updated KC (1977-1978).
centura.australian_market_notes: The Centura's Australian introduction was famously sabotaged by history: in 1973, French union wharf bans in protest of French atmospheric nuclear testing in the South Pacific delayed imported Simca bodyshell shipments for over twelve months. Unassembled bodyshells weathered on Adelaide wharves before assembly commenced in 1975. Despite this, Australian performance drivers loved the car's sensational straight-line speed, and it enjoyed a formidable track career in production car rallying and circuit racing.

sigma.overview: The Chrysler Sigma—later renamed Mitsubishi Sigma after Mitsubishi acquired Chrysler Australia in 1980—was the undisputed king of Australia's four-cylinder family car market across the late 1970s and 1980s. Manufactured at Tonsley Park in Adelaide, the Sigma (GE, GH, GJ, GK, GN) dethroned traditional six-cylinder cars by offering expansive interior space, European-influenced styling, four-wheel coil spring suspension, and revolutionary 'Silent Shaft' counter-rotating balance shafts in its Australian-cast Astron 1.85L, 2.0L, and 2.6L engines. sigma.australian_market_notes: The Sigma completely altered Australian buying habits, proving that a smooth, balance-shaft four-cylinder car could equal or exceed a traditional Australian straight-six in refinement and towing capability. charger.name: Chrysler Valiant Charger
charger.overview: The Chrysler Valiant Charger is one of the most charismatic muscle cars in Australian history. Launched in August 1971 with the memorable 'Hey Charger!' television advertising campaign, the Charger was built on a shortened 105-inch wheelbase with stunning fastback proportions, winning the 1971 Wheels Car of the Year award. Immortalized by the legendary Bathurst homologation specials—the E38 (280 bhp) and the triple-Weber E49 'Six Pack' (302 bhp)—the Charger was the fastest-accelerating Australian production car for over a decade, holding the standing quarter-mile record at 14.4 seconds.
charger.australian_market_notes: Engineered under John Ellis by chopping 6 inches out of the VH sedan wheelbase and styling an aerodynamic fastback tail, the Charger captured 50% of all Australian sports coupe sales in its first year. generations.generation_name: Galant GA, GB, GC, GD Series
generations.summary: 1.3L, 1.4L, and 1.6L Saturn engines, followed by 2.0L Astron; high build quality and rallying success.

scorpion.name: Chrysler Scorpion
scorpion.overview: Stylish 2-door pillarless sports coupe based on the Mitsubishi Sapporo, offering luxury grand-touring features.

generations.summary: 2.0L and 2.6L Astron engines with balance shafts, 5-speed manual or 3-speed auto, 4-wheel disc brakes.

chrysler-300c.name: Chrysler 300C
chrysler-300c.overview: Brawny American rear-wheel-drive luxury sedan with gangsta proportions, packing 5.7L Hemi V8 and 6.4L SRT-8 performance.

generations.summary: 3.5L/3.6L Pentastar V6, 3.0L CRD diesel, 5.7L Hemi V8, and 350kW 6.4L Hemi V8 SRT; final rear-drive V8 rival to Falcon and Commodore.

pt-cruiser.name: Chrysler PT Cruiser
pt-cruiser.overview: Retro-styled multi-purpose hatchback inspired by 1930s American hot rods, featuring versatile seating and cabriolet option.

generations.summary: 2.0L and 2.4L petrol engines, 2.4L Turbo GT (164kW), 25-way interior seat combinations.

crossfire.name: Chrysler Crossfire
crossfire.overview: Striking German-built sports car manufactured by Karmann in Osnabruck, sharing 80% of its components with the Mercedes-Benz SLK (R170).

generations.summary: Mercedes 3.2L 18-valve V6 (160kW) and supercharged SRT-6 (246kW), speed-sensitive deployable rear spoiler.

voyager.name: Chrysler Voyager / Grand Voyager
voyager.overview: The pioneer of the modern minivan, offering Stow 'n Go fold-into-the-floor seating and power sliding doors across GS, RG, and RT generations.

generations.summary: 3.3L and 3.8L V6 petrol, 2.8L CRD turbo-diesel, Stow 'n Go seating system.

sebring.name: Chrysler Sebring
sebring.overview: American mid-size car offered in four-door sedan and two-door cabriolet featuring a three-piece folding steel hardtop.

generations.summary: 2.4L World Gas Engine and 2.7L V6 petrol; retractable hardtop cabriolet.

neon.name: Chrysler Neon
neon.overview: Cab-forward American compact car with perky performance from its standard 2.0L 16-valve engine.

generations.summary: 2.0L SOHC (98kW) and DOHC (112kW) engines, frameless door glass, SE and LE trims.
